source_text: Ἀρκούσης δὲ καὶ μόνης τῆς ἐπὶ τῇ γενέσει τῶν ἀνθρώπων θεωρουμένης αἰτίας δεῖξαι τὴν ἀνάστασιν κατὰ φυσικὴν ἀκολουθίαν ἑπομένην τοῖς διαλυθεῖσι σώμασι, δίκαιον ἴσως πρὸς μηδὲν ἀποκνῆσαι τῶν προτεθέντων, ἀκολούθως δὲ τοῖς εἰρημένοις καὶ τὰς ἐξ ἑκάστου τῶν ἑπομένων ἀφορμὰς ὑποδεῖξαι τοῖς ἐξ αὐτῶν συνιδεῖν μὴ δυναμένοις, καὶ πρό γε τῶν ἄλλων τὴν τῶν γενομένων ἀνθρώπων φύσιν, ἐπὶ τὴν αὐτὴν ἄγουσαν ἔννοιαν καὶ τὴν ἴσην παρέχουσαν περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως πίστιν. Εἰ γὰρ πᾶσα κοινῶς ἡ τῶν ἀνθρώπων φύσις ἐκ ψυχῆς ἀθανάτου καὶ τοῦ κατὰ τὴν γένεσιν αὐτῇ συναρμοσθέντος σώματος ἔχει τὴν σύστασιν, καὶ μήτε τῇ φύσει τῆς ψυχῆς καθ᾿ ἑαυτὴν μήτε τῇ φύσει τοῦ σώματος χωρὶς ἀπεκλήρωσε θεὸς τὴν τοιάνδε γένεσιν ἢ τὴν ζωὴν καὶ τὸν σύμπαντα βίον, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ἐκ τούτων γενομένοις ἀνθρώποις, ἵν᾿ ἐξ ὧν γεννῶνται καὶ ζῶσι διαβιώσαντες εἰς ἕν τι καὶ κοινὸν καταλήξωσι τέλος, δεῖ πάντως ἑνὸς ὄντος ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων ζώου, τοῦ καὶ πάσχοντος ὁπόσα πάθη ψυχῆς καὶ ὁπόσα τοῦ σώματος, ἐνεργοῦντός τε καὶ πράττοντος ὁπόσα τῆς αἰσθητικῆς ἢ τῆς λογικῆς δεῖται κρίσεως, πρὸς ἕν τι τέλος ἀναφέρεσθαι πάντα τὸν ἐκ τούτων εἱρμόν, ἵνα πάντα καὶ διὰ πάντων συντρέχῃ πρὸς μίαν ἁρμονίαν καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν συμπάθειαν, ἀνθρώπου γένεσις, ἀνθρώπου φύσις, ἀνθρώπου ζωή, ἀνθρώπου πράξεις καὶ πάθη, καὶ βίος καὶ τὸ τῇ φύσει προσῆκον τέλος. Εἰ δὲ μία τίς ἐστιν ἁρμονία τοῦ ζώου παντὸς καὶ συμπάθεια, καὶ τῶν ἐκ ψυχῆς φυομένων καὶ τῶν διὰ τοῦ σώματος ἐπιτελουμένων, ἓν εἶναι δεῖ καὶ τὸ ἐπὶ πᾶσι τούτοις τέλος. Ἓν δὲ τέλος ἔσται κατ᾿ ἀλήθειαν, τοῦ αὐτοῦ ζώου κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ σύστασιν ὄντος, οὗπέρ ἐστι τέλος τὸ τέλος. Τὸ αὐτὸ δὲ ζῶον ἔσται καθαρῶς, τῶν αὐτῶν ὄντων πάντων ἐξ ὦν ὡς μερῶν τὸ ζῶον. Τὰ αὐτὰ δὲ κατὰ τὴν ἰδιάζουσαν ἕνωσιν ἔσται, τῶν διαλυθέντων πάλιν ἑνωθέντων πρὸς τὴν τοῦ ζώου σύστασιν. Ἡ δὲ τῶν αὐτῶν ἀνθρώπων σύστασις ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἑπομένην δείκνυσι τὴν τῶν νεκρωθέντων καὶ διαλυθέντων σωμάτων ἀνάστασιν· ταύτης γὰρ χωρὶς οὔτ᾿ ἂν ἑνωθείη τὰ αὐτὰ μέρη κατὰ φύσιν ἀλλήλοις, οὔτ᾿ ἂν συσταίη τῶν αὐτῶν ἀνθρώπων ἡ φύσις. Εἰ δὲ καὶ νοῦς καὶ λόγος δέδοται τοῖς ἀνθρώποις πρὸς διάκρισιν νοητῶν, οὐκ οὐσιῶν μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς τοῦ δόντος ἀγαθότητος καὶ σοφίας καὶ δικαιοσύνης, ἀνάγκη, διαμενόντων ὦν ἕνεκεν ἡ λογικὴ δέδοται κρίσις, καὶ αὐτὴν διαμένειν τὴν ἐπὶ τούτοις δοθεῖσαν κρίσιν. Ταύτην δὲ διαμένειν ἀδύνατον, μὴ τῆς δεξαμένης αὐτὴν καὶ τῆς ἐν οἶς ἐστι διαμενούσης φύσεως. Ὁ δὲ καὶ νοῦν καὶ λόγον δεξάμενός ἐστιν ἄνθρωπος, οὐ ψυχὴ καθ᾿ ἑαυτήν. Ἄνθρωπον ἄρα δεῖ τὸν ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων ὄντα διαμένειν εἰς ἀεί. Τοῦτον δὲ ἀδύνατον διαμένειν, μὴ ἀνιστάμενον. Ἀναστάσεως γὰρ μὴ γινομένης, οὐκ ἂν ἡ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ὡς ἀνθρώπων διαμένοι φύσις. Τῆς δὲ τῶν ἀνθρώπων φύσεως μὴ διαμενούσης, μάτην μὲν ἡ ψυχὴ συνήρμοσται τῇ τοῦ σώματος ἐνδείᾳ καὶ τοῖς τούτου πάθεσι, μάτην δὲ τὸ σῶμα πεπέδηται πρὸς τὸ τυγχάνειν ὦν ὀρέγεται, ταῖς τῆς ψυχῆς ἡνίαις ὑπεῖκον καὶ χαλιναγωγούμενον, μάταιος δὲ ὁ νοῦς, ματαία δὲ φρόνησις, καὶ δικαιοσύνης παρατήρησις, ἢ καὶ πάσης ἀρετῆς ἄσκησις, καὶ νόμων θέσις καὶ διάταξις, καὶ συνόλως εἰπεῖν πᾶν ὅ τι περ ἐν ἀνθρώποις καὶ δι᾿ ἀνθρώπους καλόν, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ αὐτὴ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἡ γένεσίς τε καὶ φύσις. Εἰ δὲ πάντων καὶ πανταχόθεν ἀπελήλαται τῶν ἔργων τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τῶν ὑπ᾿ ἐκεῖνου διδομένων δωρεῶν τὸ μάταιον, δεῖ πάντως τῷ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀτελευτήτῳ συνδιαιωνίζειν τὴν τοῦ σώματος διαμονὴν κατὰ τὴν οἰκείαν φύσιν.
pass_a_gloss: It is sufficient to show the resurrection following naturally to the bodies that have been dissolved, based on the cause observed in the generation of humans, and it is right not to omit any of the things previously proposed, but to also show the starting points from each of the things that follow, for those who are not able to understand from the things themselves, and before all else, the nature of the humans who have come into being, leading to the same notion and providing equal faith about the resurrection. For if the entire human nature in general has its composition from an immortal soul and the body which is harmoniously joined to it from the beginning, and neither did God complete this kind of generation or life or the entire life for the nature of the soul by itself or for the nature of the body by itself, but for the humans who have come into being from these, so that having been generated and lived from the things from which they are generated, they may arrive at one common end, it is necessary that there is one living being composed of both, which both suffers the things that the soul suffers and the things that the body suffers, and is active and does the things that require the judgment of the senses or the intellect, all being referred to one end, so that all things may run together through all things to one harmony and the same sympathy, the generation of a human, the nature of a human, the life of a human, the actions and passions of a human, and the life and the end that belongs to nature. And if there is one harmony and sympathy of the entire living being, and of the things that grow from the soul and the things that are accomplished through the body, it is necessary that there is also one end for all these things. And there will be one end in truth, of the same living being, existing according to its own composition, for which the end is the end. The same living being will exist, composed of the same things, of which the living being is composed as parts. The same things will exist, according to their own special union, of the things that have been dissolved and then reunited for the composition of the living being. The composition of the same humans necessarily shows the resurrection of the bodies that have died and been dissolved, for without this, neither would the same parts be united naturally to each other, nor would the nature of the same humans be composed. And if intellect and reason have been given to humans for the distinction of intelligible things, not only of substances but also of the goodness and wisdom and justice of the one who gives, it is necessary, since the rational judgment has been given for the sake of remaining, that this judgment also remains, and it is impossible for it to remain without the nature that has received it and in which it exists remaining. The one who has received intellect and reason is a human, not a soul by itself. Therefore, it is necessary for the human, who exists from both, to remain forever. It is impossible for this human to remain without rising again. For if the resurrection does not occur, the nature of humans as humans will not remain. And if the nature of humans does not remain, the soul has been joined to the body's need and its passions in vain, and the body has been bound to attain the things it desires, being yielded to and controlled by the soul's reins, and the intellect is vain, and prudence is vain, and the observance of justice, or the practice of any virtue, and the establishment and arrangement of laws, and in general, all that is good among humans and through humans, or rather even the generation and nature of humans themselves. But if the vain thing has been eliminated from all the works of God and the gifts given by him, it is necessary that the immortality of the soul coexists with the remaining of the body, according to its own nature.

pass_b_english: The cause observed in human generation alone is enough to prove the resurrection follows naturally for dissolved bodies. It is right not to omit any of the points already proposed, but to also set out the starting points from each consequence for those who cannot grasp them from the things themselves. Above all, the nature of the humans who have come into being leads to the same conception and provides equal faith concerning the resurrection. For if the whole of human nature in general has its composition from an immortal soul and the body harmoniously fitted to it at generation, and God did not complete this kind of generation or life or the entire life for the nature of the soul by itself or for the nature of the body by itself, but for the humans generated from these, so that after being born and living from what they are born from they may reach one common end, then there must be one living being composed of both. This living being suffers all the passions of the soul and all the passions of the body, acts and performs whatever requires sensory or rational judgment, and refers everything to one end, so that all things run together through all things toward one harmony and the same sympathy: human generation, human nature, human life, human actions and passions, and life and the end proper to nature. If there is one harmony and sympathy for the whole living being, both for what springs from the soul and what is accomplished through the body, there must also be one end over all these things. There will be one true end for the same living being existing according to its own composition, for which the end is the end. The same living being will exist purely when the same elements of which the living being consists as parts are present. The same elements will exist in their proper union when the dissolved parts are reunited for the living being's composition. The composition of the same humans necessarily proves the resurrection of the dead and dissolved bodies; without it the same parts would not be naturally united to one another, nor would the nature of the same humans be constituted. If intellect and reason have been given to humans to discern intelligible things — not only substances but also the goodness, wisdom, and justice of the Giver — then, since rational judgment was given for the sake of remaining, that judgment must itself remain. But it cannot remain unless the nature that received it and in which it exists also remains. The one who received intellect and reason is a human, not a soul by itself. Therefore the human composed of both must remain forever. Yet this human cannot remain without rising again; if resurrection does not occur, the nature of humans as humans will not remain. And if human nature does not remain, the soul has been joined to the body's need and its passions in vain, the body has been yoked to attain what it desires, yielding to the soul's reins and controlled by them, in vain; intellect is vain, prudence is vain, the observance of justice is vain, the practice of any virtue is vain, the establishment and ordering of laws is vain, and in short every good thing among humans and through humans — or rather, the very generation and nature of humans themselves. But if the vain has been banished from all the works of God and from the gifts He gives, then the deathlessness of the soul must co-eternally share the body's continuance according to its own nature.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex philosophical arguments regarding the composition of human nature and the necessity of resurrection. Pass A preserves all clauses and nuances of the Greek, and Pass B is a faithful rendering that does not add or contradict the source. All logical connections (causality, necessity, and the relationship between soul and body) are maintained.
